2013: Alice Munro (Canada) – short story collections: "Dance of the Happy Shades", "The Beggar Maid", "Runaway".

2014: Patrick Modiano (France) – notable works: "Missing Person", "Dora Bruder", "The Search for the Last Train".

**Nobel Prize in Literature – Laureates (2010‑2015) & Their Best‑Known Works** | Year | Laureate | Country (citizenship at award) | Most‑famous work(s) – why they stand out | |------|----------|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------------| | **2010** | **Mario Vargas Llosa** | Peru (also Spanish citizenship) | • *The Time of the Hero* (1963) – his first novel, a powerful critique of military academy life in Peru.
• *The War of the End of the World* (1981) – a sweeping historical novel based on the 19th‑century Brazilian revolt.
• *Conversation in the Cathedral* (1969) – a landmark of Latin‑American “Boom” literature, exploring political repression and personal betrayal. | | **2011** | **Tomas Tranströmer** | Sweden | • *The Great Enigma* (1992) – a celebrated collection that showcases his signature spare, image‑rich poetry.
• *Baltics* (1974) – another key anthology that established his reputation for blending nature, myth, and existential depth.
*(Tranströmer is primarily a poet; his fame rests on his collected poems rather than a single book.)* | | **2012** | **Mo Yan** | China | • *Red Sorghum* (1986) – the novel that launched his international reputation; later adapted into an acclaimed film.
• *Big Breasts and Wide Hips* (1995) – a multigenerational saga of a Chinese family during the 20th‑century upheavals.
• *Life and Death Are Wearing Me Out* (2006) – a satirical, reincarnation‑spanning epic that blends folklore with modern history. | | **2013** | **Alice Munro** | Canada | • *Dance of the Happy Shades* (1968) – her first collection, winner of the Governor General’s Award.
• *The Beggar Maid* (1978) (also published as *Who Do You Think You Are?*) – a masterful linked‑story novel about a woman’s rise from a small town to the city.
• *Runaway* (2004) – a later collection that reaffirmed her status as the pre‑eminent contemporary short‑story writer. | | **2014** | **Patrick Modiano** | France | • *Missing Person* (1978) – the novel that earned him the Prix Goncourt; a haunting exploration of identity and memory in post‑war Paris.
• *Dora Bruder* (1997) – a blend of biography and fiction that tracks a missing Jewish girl during the Occupation.
• *The Search for the Last Train* (2001) – another quintessential Modiano work, dealing with the lingering shadows of the Holocaust and personal loss. | | **2015** | **Svetlana Alexievich** | Belarus (by birth; Russian‑language writer) | • *War’s Unwomanly Face* (1985) – oral histories of Soviet women who served in World War II, groundbreaking for its testimonial style.
• *Chernobyl Prayer* (1997) (also titled *Voices from Chernobyl*) – a moving collage of first‑hand accounts of the 1986 disaster.
• *Secondhand Time* (2013) – a sweeping portrait of post‑Soviet life told through the voices of ordinary citizens. | **Quick take‑aways** * The laureates span a wide range of genres: novels, short‑story collections, poetry, and oral‑history documentary literature. * Several winners (Tranströmer, Alexievich) are known more for a body of work or a distinctive method (poetry, oral testimony) than for a single “title.” * All of the listed works are repeatedly cited in literary criticism, award citations, and popular media as the authors’ most recognizable or influential contributions.
